title: The Ethics of Species Triage
paragraphs: Conservation organizations facing genuinely limited resources increasingly confront the uncomfortable necessity of species triage, prioritizing certain endangered species for intensive protection while effectively accepting that others will likely receive insufficient resources to prevent eventual extinction.

This triage approach generates genuine ethical discomfort, as prioritization criteria, whether based on ecological function, genetic uniqueness, or public appeal, inevitably involve value judgments that implicitly rank different species' relative worth in ways many conservation professionals find personally troubling.

Critics argue that explicit triage risks becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy, whereby species deemed lower priority receive even less attention and resources than their situation might otherwise generate, potentially accelerating extinction that more equal resource distribution might have prevented.

Defenders counter that implicit triage already occurs regardless of explicit acknowledgment, since limited conservation resources inevitably distribute unevenly across species regardless of whether this distribution follows deliberate strategic criteria or simply reflects historical accident and public attention patterns.

This argument suggests that explicit, deliberate triage criteria, however uncomfortable, likely produces better aggregate conservation outcomes than implicit, unexamined resource distribution patterns that occur without deliberate strategic consideration regardless of whether decision-makers acknowledge this reality.

This uncomfortable necessity reflects a broader pattern in conservation ethics, where limited resources force painful prioritization decisions that comfortable abstraction regarding equal species value cannot practically accommodate given genuine resource constraints facing contemporary conservation efforts.
